text: The tactics selected for this strategy are to (1) leverage the project’s commissioning NEPA review to retire MTV-specific in-service regulatory considerations as well as to define best management practices, (2) identify and secure possible pre-authorizations, (3) compile data and analyses to be provided to regulators and resource managers to expedite review, and (4) the strategy could also include securing pre-approvals for specific site/CEC combinations if the first users of the MTV are committed in advance but is dependent on project NEPA outcomes, customer commitment(s), as well as remaining project resources. Ultimately, identifying and fully securing regulatory approvals for using the MTV for CEC testing must be addressed case-by-case, focusing on un-retired risks (CEC and site-specific risks). For each MTV use request, gaps in previously secured and required regulatory approvals must be determined, a plan must be developed to address those gaps, and a process must be followed to secure approvals. DOE’s Testing & Expertise for Marine Energy (TEAMER)5 program offers support for “open water” testing of marine energy systems. It has developed a process to evaluate project regulatory risk, especially to gauge the time required to secure approvals. Due to the success of this approach, alignment with DOE NEPA processes, and applicability to MTV use, a similar process is proposed for in-service MTV use: 1) An environmental consultant will be retained to review the proposed MTV use details and make a preliminary assessment of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) or Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) expected effects based upon requested in-service site(s) and CEC(s). 2) The consultant will assist in assessing likely findings under Section 7 of the ESA and recommend alternative methods or scope changes to achieve a finding of “No Effect” or “Not Likely to Adversely Affect.” 5 https://teamer-us.org Final Technical Report 44/57 3) The environmental consultant will work with the MTV’s owner and user to prepare a BE (if additional NEPA review or regulatory agency consultation is required) and assist the lead regulatory agency in helping secure concurrence and final determination(s). 4) The environmental consultant will also assist with securing any permit(s) needed for the MTV testing campaign. 5) Subsequent MTV use can leverage prior efforts by systematically retiring regulatory risks and building regulatory agency trust. Several in-service regulatory strategy tactics were also defined to minimize further effort, cost, and time required before each utilization. Tactic 1: Leverage the project’s NEPA process To commission the MTV with DOE support, DOE NEPA authorization is needed. This process will be the first to explore detailed federal, state, and local regulatory considerations associated with using the MTV for CEC testing. Although these authorizations will be for MTV use at a site(s) and deploying a CEC(s) specific to commissioning, future use will build upon the developed foundation. Any eligible pre-authorizations that could be secured will be exposed, and data/analyses used for the DOE NEPA process (including any NEPA compliance documents created) will constitute the basis for a portfolio of information useful in expediting future approvals.
